source: Li et al. (2024) Do Machines and Humans Focus on Similar Code? Explainability of LLMs in Code Summarization (ICPC)
finding: SHAP-based model focus on code tokens does not match human eye-tracking focus when summarizing Java. Alignment also did not predict summary quality.
numbers: 6 models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, GPT-3.5 few-shot, StarCoder, Code Llama, NCS); 27 programmers, 671 trials, 68 Java methods. At most 22% of methods had significant human-LLM Spearman rho; 85% for LLM-LLM pairs. Duration vs GPT-4 mean rho -0.11 +/- 0.41. Alignment vs accuracy rho -0.128 p=0.39; completeness 0.131 p=0.38.
quote: we find no statistically significant evidence suggesting the hypothesized alignment
limits: Black-box SHAP only; Java only; one expert rater; low power.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the model reads code where a human reads it. Do not use model attention as a proxy for comprehension.

source: Kou et al. (2024) Do LLMs Pay Similar Attention Like Human Programmers When Generating Code? (FSE)
finding: Across 6 LLMs, attention on the task description differs from what human programmers mark as important. Misalignment explains part of the errors.
numbers: HumanEval 164 + MBPP 974 tasks labelled by 2 programmers (Cohen kappa 0.68-0.73). Best method BERT masking: top-5 F1 45.7%, alpha 0.27 (below 0.3 for all). GPT-4 lowest, F1 30.0%, alpha 0.04. 211 wrong programs: 57 (27%) explained by five attention patterns (CodeGen 31%, GPT-4 8%). Mapping NL words to code was the largest pattern (25 of 57).
quote: a consistent misalignment between LLMs' and programmers' attention
limits: Python only; perturbation was the only method usable for GPT-4; user study N=22 (14 of 22 still distrusted LLMs).
agent_relevance: A comprehension step that forces the agent to restate conditions, data types and operations from the task could cover missed attention. Stronger models show less pattern-explained error.

source: Paltenghi et al. (2022) Thinking Like a Developer? Comparing the Attention of Humans with Neural Models of Code
finding: Model attention correlates only weakly with developer gaze during code sensemaking. A follow-up-attention method predicts the next line a developer views better than a developer-history baseline.
numbers: 25 developers, 92 eye-tracking sessions, 45 tasks (Python, C++, C#). Spearman model vs human: CodeGen 16B +0.22, InCoder 6B +0.20, GPT-J 6B +0.04; developer vs developer +0.56. Follow-up attention: Spearman 0.49, top-3 overlap 47% vs 42.3% baseline. Answers correct or partial: developers about 70%, CodeGen 39.3%, GPT-J 36.3%, InCoder 37.7%.
quote: follow-up attention performs best among all methods for both Spearman rank and top-3 overlap
limits: One company; sensemaking tasks not debugging; open models only; CodeGen only for RQ4-5; paper text read to about 100k characters.
agent_relevance: Human reading order (which line next) is partly predictable from what was just read. A navigation policy could use follow-up links instead of raw similarity.

source: EEG study of confusion (2025, authors not confirmed) Are Humans and LLMs Confused by the Same Code? Fixation-Related Potentials and LLM Perplexity (ICSE 2026)
finding: LLM token perplexity is higher on code snippets with atoms of confusion and tracks the human EEG confusion signal on those snippets.
numbers: 24 EEG participants, 1432 usable trials, 72 clean/confusing pairs. Main model Qwen2.5-Coder-32B. Max perplexity per area of interest, confusing vs clean: r=0.45, p<0.001. Perplexity vs late frontal positivity: rho=0.47 (p<0.001) on confusing code, rho=0.05 (ns) on clean. Data-driven perplexity peaks found about 64% of labelled atoms; 69-85 novel regions (text gives two counts).
quote: LLM perplexity spikes correlate both in terms of location and amplitude with human neurophysiological responses
limits: Java only, intermediate programmers, few epochs per atom, hypothesis not proven.
agent_relevance: Perplexity spikes can be a cheap confusion detector: lines where the model itself is surprised are candidates for a second read or a trace. Needs testing on bug lines.

source: Predicting Program Comprehension with Foundation Models of Human Cognition (2026, under review, authors not confirmed)
finding: Centaur (Llama 3.1 fine-tuned on 160 psychology experiments) predicts human response distributions in 9 published comprehension studies more closely than base Llama 3.1.
numbers: Abstract only: no numbers given. Centaur less dependent on prior trials than the base model.
quote: more closely aligns with human response patterns than its base model
limits: Abstract read only; under review; no effect sizes available.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. Note as a lead; do not rely.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) Unveiling the Magic of Code Reasoning through Reflective Hypothesis Decomposition and Amendment (ICLR)
finding: A loop of propose hypothesis, run a tool to check, then amend lifts code-reasoning scores. Plain CoT already gives most of the gain on deductive tasks.
numbers: Deductive code reasoning, CRUXEval / LiveCodeBench: standard 68.75 / 41.18; CoT 89.12 / 83.14; self-consistency N=3 71.12 / 36.27; self-refine T=2 80.38 / 63.73; chain-of-code 85.62 / 81.37; RHDA T=2 N=1 90.62 / 84.16; without amend 86.62 / 71.29. Abductive (input prediction) is harder. Claim of gains up to 3x.
limits: Gain over CoT on deductive is only about 1.5 to 1 points on CRUXEval; LiveCodeBench subset small.
agent_relevance: Execution-style comprehension: step-by-step trace beats voting (self-consistency hurt on LiveCodeBench). Tool-checked hypotheses add a few points. Fits G2 and G4.

source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval: A Benchmark for Code Reasoning, Understanding and Execution
finding: 800 short Python functions test output prediction and input prediction. Chain of thought helps strong models; no model solves it.
numbers: Pass@1 input / output: GPT-4 without CoT 67 / 63, with CoT 74.8 / 81.9; Code Llama 34B direct 46.5 / 41.1; Phi-1 13.9 / 23.3. Fine-tuning Code Llama 34B on about 140K distilled samples roughly matches GPT-4 but plateaus below 70%. CoT does not help Code Llama 13B or GPT-3.5 on input prediction. Models distilled for HumanEval (WizardCoder, Phind, Phi) score far higher on HumanEval but do not beat Code Llama 34B here.
limits: Short single-model-generated functions; differences under 1.5 points are noise; public data so possible contamination; first 100k characters read.
agent_relevance: Mentally executing code is separable from writing code. CoT for tracing helps only above some capability level; test per model.

source: Semantics-preserving mutation study (2025, authors not confirmed) Are Large Language Models Robust in Understanding Code Against Semantics-Preserving Mutations?
finding: Models predict outputs right for wrong reasons. Semantics-preserving edits (rename, mirror, swap branches, loop rewrite) change answers.
numbers: Six models up to 8B on LiveCodeBench (479) and CRUXEval (800). Single-mutation accuracy drops up to 7-8 points (if-else swap, unrolling). Correct predictions with flawed reasoning on LiveCodeBench: Llama3.2 60.9%, CodeGemma 51.4%, Mistral 49.7%, GraniteCode 42.3%, SemCoder 16.1%, Qwen2.5-Coder 12.8%.
quote: indicating limited robustness in their semantic understanding
limits: Models only up to 8B; Python; five mutations; reasoning audit on LiveCodeBench only; prose and table numbers disagree.
agent_relevance: A pass on one phrasing of a program is not proof of understanding. Mutate the code and re-trace (G3). Check reasoning, not just the answer.

source: CodeSense (2025) A Real-World Benchmark and Dataset for Code Semantic Reasoning
finding: Fine-grained semantic questions on real projects are hard for 14 LLMs. Accuracy falls fast as the statement block grows.
numbers: 744 projects (Python, C, Java), 4,483 samples. Single C statements: Claude 3.5 and GPT-4o-mini under 30%; no model above 50% on Python single statements. 3-statement Python blocks about 20% (Claude 3.5), C under 10%. Input prediction best model about 12% on small functions. API definitions added: Qwen2.5-7B 0.206 to 0.226, Phi-4 0.125 to 0.089. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B abstract-value prediction 0.169 (random) -> 0.316 (0-shot) -> 0.784 (3-shot). Simple CoT helps little.
quote: the lack of code semantics in LLMs fundamentally limit models' capabilities of code reasoning
limits: Exact match only; primitive types; repositories may be in training data; model list is mid-2025.
agent_relevance: Fine-grained value tracking is a real weakness. Retrieved matching examples help more than CoT or documentation. Run code instead of predicting values.

source: RepoNavigator (2025, authors not confirmed) One Tool Is Enough: RL for Repository-Level LLM Agents
finding: A single tool (jump to symbol definition via language server) trained with RL localises issues better than multi-tool agents. Fewer tools was better.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Instruct 7B/14B/32B. Function IoU on SWE-bench Verified: 7B 15.46 training-free to 26.43 with GRPO; 14B 23.00 to 26.84; 32B 25.16 to 32.30 (Claude-3.7 RepoNavigator 30.22). Best baseline at 14B 18.92. Tool ablation at 7B: all four tools 13.71, jump+GetClass+GetFunc 21.44, jump+GetStruc 24.00, jump alone 24.28. Resolve rate 14.74% vs Agentless 10.12%.
limits: Python only; gold-patch ground truth; Verified may leak; one baseline not reproduced; SWE-agent not in tables.
agent_relevance: Program comprehension for an agent is following definitions. A narrow def-following tool beat a broad toolbox. Keep the comprehension tool set small.

source: Chai et al. (2026) RepoNav: From Snippet Retrieval to File-Centered Repository Navigation for Code Agents
finding: Agents reach the right file but pick the wrong function in 44-58% of function-level misses. Premature anchoring on a salient symbol is the cause they name. A compact tree of sibling symbols fixes part of it.
numbers: LocBench 560 instances; GPT-OSS-120B ablation Function Acc@5: file-only 32.61, inline scaffold 46.96, tree scaffold 52.13; Rec@10 44.29 / 53.84 / 60.98. File-to-function gap 26.9 -> 21.7 points vs snippet search (paired p=0.017 and 0.007). Gemini-3-Flash gains +3.2 and +6.6 points Acc@5 over Bash and snippet. Snippet search alone gave about zero or negative change.
quote: agents often commit to a salient nearby symbol before inspecting sibling definitions
limits: Three backbones; one localisation benchmark plus a QA set; Python.
agent_relevance: Machine version of early commitment: the agent takes the first plausible symbol. Show siblings before choosing (compare alternatives on evidence). Supports an overview-before-dive step.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: A fixed three-phase pipeline (localize, repair, validate) without an agent loop beat open agents on SWE-bench Lite at low cost.
numbers: 32.00% (96 problems) on SWE-bench Lite at $0.70 per issue. Authors found some Lite items with leaked patches or misleading text and built Lite-S.
quote: Agentless employs a simplistic three-phase process of localization, repair, and patch validation
limits: Abstract only read: the file to function to line hierarchy is not checked here.
agent_relevance: Code, not the model, controls the reading order (coarse to fine). Matches schema section 1.

source: Jimenez et al. (2024) SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
finding: Real issue resolution needs long-context comprehension across files; the best 2023 model solved 1.96%.
numbers: 2,294 task instances, 12 Python repositories. Claude 2 resolved 1.96%.
limits: Abstract only read. Scores are far higher today.
agent_relevance: Reference point that cross-file comprehension was the original bottleneck.

source: Zi et al. (2025) 'I Would Have Written My Code Differently': Beginners Struggle to Understand LLM-Generated Code
finding: CS1 students checking LLM implementations against a natural-language description succeeded on only about a third of tasks.
numbers: 32 students, 160 task instances, per-task success 32.5%. Challenges: non-native English, unfamiliar syntax, automation bias.
quote: Our results show a low per-task success rate of 32.5%
limits: Abstract only read. Novices only.
agent_relevance: Readers of model-written code are weak checkers. Do not rely on a reading as the verifier; use runs.

source: Kaufman, Brun, Murali, Endres (2026) Programmers Are Poor and Overconfident Judges of LLM-Generated Assertions
finding: Programmers accept correct assertions far more often than they reject wrong ones, with equal confidence. Most used a top-down reading.
numbers: 86 programmers, controlled experiment. Correct postconditions judged correct 73.9%; incorrect judged incorrect 49.0% (p<0.001, odds ratio 2.94). Similar confidence in both. Think-aloud N=10, 50 responses: 31 top-down (docstring first; counted as 50 minus 7, 10, 2), 7 bottom-up, 10 as-needed, 2 unclear. Intuition used in 12 of 50 and was wrong in 7 of those 12.
limits: Python functions; strategy coding by one author after joint calibration on one transcript; think-aloud small. PDF text read via pdftotext.
agent_relevance: Human Brooks-style top-down reading is common and fails when the stated intent is wrong. An LLM judge reading spec then code would share that anchoring. Check by running (G3).

source: Copilot brownfield comprehension study (2025, authors not confirmed) Code Comprehension with GitHub Copilot: Performance Gains, Comprehension Trade-offs, and Behavioral Predictors
finding: Copilot sped up task completion but comprehension scores did not change. Write-then-view loops predicted comprehension.
numbers: 15 graduate students within-subject, 3,818-line JS app. Time 632 s vs 1281 s (-50.7%, p<0.0001); tests passed 7.2 vs 4.2. Comprehension 7.86/15 vs 7.27/15 (p=0.59). Performance-comprehension rho -0.29 (ns). High-comprehension group had 4.7x as many write-then-view transitions and spent 8.2% vs 24.0% of time viewing Copilot output.
quote: successful task completion does not reliably indicate code comprehension
limits: N=15, fixed condition order, short 8-item test.
agent_relevance: Task success is not understanding. A patch passing tests may rest on a wrong model of the code, so verify the model separately.

source: Qiao, Shihab, Hundhausen (2025) Systematic review of GenAI assistants for code comprehension
finding: 31 studies (2022-2024) mostly show GenAI tools help code understanding. Explanations are often incomplete or partly wrong. Novices read bottom-up, experts top-down.
numbers: 31 studies, 25 lab. Ivie 90.2% correct vs 65.0% for a GPT chatbot. GILT +0.47 subtasks vs search. CodeAid explanations accurate 95%. One line-by-line study: 90% complete but 67.2% correct. Another: 93% had a correct statement but 50% had an incorrect one.
limits: Three databases, English only, mostly lab studies.
agent_relevance: Model explanations of code are fluent but a third wrong in line-by-line settings. Treat self-generated code summaries as hypotheses, not facts.

source: EyeMulator (2026, authors not confirmed) Improving Code Language Models by Mimicking Human Visual Attention (ACL 2026)
finding: Training code models with weights derived from human eye-tracking scan paths improved completion, translation and summarization in all 36 settings.
numbers: 6 backbones x 3 CodeXGLUE tasks x 2 data regimes = 36 cells, all positive deltas. Larger for completion and translation; smaller but positive METEOR for summarization. No exact deltas read.
limits: Abstract only; needs training so not usable in a prompt-only scaffold.
agent_relevance: Human fixation is useful as a training signal; for us only an idea of which tokens matter.

source: Kou et al. (2024) user study of attention explanations
finding: Programmers preferred perturbation (SHAP) explanations of where the model looked, but most still did not trust the model.
numbers: 22 programmers, mean 5.62 years. Alignment rating SHAP 5.13, Input x Gradient 4.59, CODING_all 3.62 (7-point). SHAP vs Input x Gradient p=0.02. 14 of 22 still lacked trust.
limits: User study small, one model (CodeGen-2.7B), eight tasks.
agent_relevance: Showing the reader where the model looked does not buy trust. Evidence from execution is the better trust signal.

source: Kou et al. (2024) error analysis of attention patterns
finding: Most wrong programs from small models are not explained by missing attention; the share is larger for weak models and tiny for GPT-4.
numbers: 57 of 211 wrong programs (27%) fit a pattern. CodeGen 54 of 172 (31%); GPT-4 3 of 39 (8%). Per pattern: NL-to-code mapping 25, descriptive words 13, data types 7, conditions 6, operations 6.
limits: Manual labelling; counts from one sample.
agent_relevance: For strong models the failures are mostly elsewhere (reasoning), so a read-the-task checklist helps weak models more.

source: Paltenghi et al. (2022) answer correctness vs developers
finding: On sensemaking questions about code, 2022 open models answered far less often than developers.
numbers: Developers correct or partial about 70%; CodeGen 39.3%, InCoder 37.7%, GPT-J 36.3%.
limits: Old open models; today's models likely higher; single company.
agent_relevance: Gives a historic baseline for human vs model code question answering. Do not transfer to 2026 models.

source: Copilot brownfield study (2025) behavioral predictors
finding: Within the Copilot condition, the participants who understood the code best wrote code themselves and checked it, rather than reading generated output.
numbers: High-comprehension n=8 vs low n=7. Write-then-view transitions 10.8 vs 2.3 (4.7x, p=0.001). Time viewing Copilot responses 8.2% vs 24.0%; time writing 20.6% vs 10.7%.
limits: Median split, n=15, associative only.
agent_relevance: Active generate-then-check beats passive reading, which matches the schema's run-and-compare stance.

source: CodeSense (2025) prompting effects
finding: Few-shot examples, especially retrieved matching ones, lifted semantic prediction far more than CoT or API documentation.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B 0.316 0-shot to 0.784 3-shot on abstract-value prediction. API definitions: Qwen2.5-7B +0.020, Phi-4 -0.036. CoT little help on statement prediction but helped loop prediction for some.
limits: Exact match scoring; tasks were synthetic probes of real code.
agent_relevance: If a comprehension step is used, give worked traces of similar code rather than more documentation.

source: RepoNavigator (2025) tool-count ablation
finding: Giving the agent more navigation tools lowered localization after RL: one jump tool beat four tools.
numbers: 7B function IoU: four tools 13.71; jump+GetClass+GetFunc 21.44; jump+GetStruc 24.00; jump only 24.28. More allowed turns helped before and after RL (figure only).
limits: Python only; Qwen 7B; trained policy, not prompt-only.
agent_relevance: Do not add comprehension tools to the schema without an ablation (G7).

source: Kaufman et al. (2026) reasoning strategies and intuition
finding: Five reasoning strategies were seen when checking assertions: clause comparison, logic walk-through, positive example, negative example, intuition. Intuition-only answers were mostly wrong.
numbers: Think-aloud 10 participants, 50 responses. Intuition in 12/50; 7 of those 12 wrong; they made up the majority of the 11 incorrect responses. Negative examples mainly used to confirm suspected errors.
limits: Small qualitative sample; exploratory.
agent_relevance: Matches G3: examples chosen after suspicion confirm; they do not find. Ban answer-by-intuition for verification.
